perf: Use Arc<StoreValue> to eliminate clone overhead

- Change Store to use Arc<StoreValue> instead of StoreValue
- Update all query functions to return Arc<StoreValue>
- Predicate indices now work with Arc<StoreValue>
- Use Arc::unwrap_or_clone() when converting to gRPC responses
- Eliminates expensive StoreValue clones on every query result
- Memory overhead: +16 bytes per entry (Arc ref counts)
- Performance: Zero-cost clones (just pointer + atomic increment)

perf(db): use Arc<StoreKey> to avoid cloning vectors on queries

Wrap StoreKey in Arc to eliminate expensive vector clones on query results.
Query allocations reduced from 7.85GB to 955MB (87.8% reduction).

fix: wrap papaya collection constructors in catch_unwind to prevent silent crashes (#339)

* utils: add fallible module for papaya concurrent collection initialization

Papaya's HashMap::new() and HashSet::new() are lazy: the internal hash
table is not allocated until the first insert(). This deferral means
that an assertion panic (assert!(len.is_power_of_two())) or an OOM
allocation failure surfaces at an arbitrary mutation point rather than
at construction time, making the root cause harder to diagnose.

Introduce utils::fallible with four helpers that force immediate
pre-allocation via with_capacity(1) inside catch_unwind, converting
panics into Results:

  - try_new_hashmap    -> Result<ConcurrentHashMap<K, V>, String>
  - try_new_arc_hashmap -> Result<Arc<ConcurrentHashMap<K, V>>, String>
  - try_new_hashset    -> Result<ConcurrentHashSet<T>, String>
  - try_new_hashset_with_capacity -> Result<ConcurrentHashSet<T>, String>

A module-level usage table guides callers on when to use Result
propagation (server startup, before panic-hook install) vs. expect()
(inside tasks, after panic-hook install).

Include 26 tests covering happy paths, type variants (string keys,
custom Hash+Eq keys), concurrency (16-thread parallel construction,
shared read/write, 1000-entry stress), capacity edge cases (0, 1,
10_000), repeated create/drop cycles (100 iterations to detect
collector-state leaks), catch_unwind integration, and reserve
after fallible init.

* utils: make ClientHandler construction fallible via catch_unwind

The ClientHandler constructor used ConcurrentHashSet::with_capacity
directly, leaving any papaya initialization panic uncatchable.
Since this runs at server startup, before the panic hook is installed,
an abort would be noisy and inscrutable.

Wrap the HashSet creation in catch_unwind via fallible::
try_new_hashset_with_capacity. On failure, print a descriptive fatal
error to stderr and abort, giving operators a clear signal that the
server cannot continue.

* db: wrap StoreHandler and Store papaya init in catch_unwind

StoreHandler::new() creates an Arc<ConcurrentHashMap> at server startup,
before the panic hook is installed. A raw papaya HashMap::new() would
defer allocation to the first insert, making any failure land at an
unpredictable point.

Use fallible::try_new_arc_hashmap with unwrap_or_else + abort to
surface failures immediately with a clear fatal message.

Store::create() runs inside tasks after the panic hook is active, so
use fallible::try_new_hashmap with expect() — the hook will catch any
re-panic.

This is part of fixing GitHub issue #318 (papaya hashmap init crash).

* db: wrap NonLinearAlgorithmIndices papaya init in catch_unwind

NonLinearAlgorithmIndices::create() constructs a ConcurrentHashMap for
algorithm-to-index mappings. This runs at store-creation time, after the
panic hook is installed, so a re-panic via catch_unwind + expect is the
correct pattern.

Use fallible::try_new_hashmap to force immediate pre-allocation and
surface any papaya initialization panic at the construction site with
a descriptive message.

Part of GitHub issue #318 and #100 (fallible collections).

* db: wrap PredicateIndices and PredicateIndex papaya init in catch_unwind

Three papaya constructors in the predicate module were using bare
new() calls, deferring allocation failure to the first mutation:

  - PredicateIndices::init() creates both a ConcurrentHashSet for
    allowed_predicates and an InnerPredicateIndices map.
  - PredicateIndex::init() creates an InnerPredicateIndex map.
  - PredicateIndex::add() creates per-key ConcurrentHashSets inside
    a parallel for_each.

All three now use fallible::try_new_hashmap / try_new_hashset with
expect(), since they run under the panic hook.  The parallel code-path
additionally benefits from catch_unwind wrapping across rayon threads.

Part of GitHub issues #318 and #100.

* ai: wrap AIStoreHandler papaya init in catch_unwind

AIStoreHandler::new() constructs an Arc<ConcurrentHashMap> at server
startup, before the panic hook is installed. A raw papaya HashMap::new()
defers allocation to the first insert, making any failure hard to
diagnose.

Use fallible::try_new_hashmap with unwrap_or_else + abort to surface
failures immediately with a clear fatal message.

Part of GitHub issues #318 and #100.

* similarity: wrap HNSW papaya HashMap init in catch_unwind

The HNSW index uses papaya ConcurrentHashMaps for its graph and nodes
tables. Seven construction sites across new_with_config, Default::default,
and From impls used raw HashMap::new(), deferring allocation failure.

Add a private new_hashmap() helper that forces immediate allocation via
with_capacity(1) inside catch_unwind with expect(). Since these
constructors run at runtime after the panic hook is installed, a
re-panic from the expect is caught gracefully and reported.

Part of GitHub issues #318 and #100.

Fix inverted HNSW ordering for cosine and dot product (#380)

* Fix inverted HNSW ordering for cosine and dot product

HNSW compares as smaller-is-closer everywhere, but cosine and dot product
return similarities where larger is closer, so both graph construction and
search ranked results backwards. Recall on SIFT was 0.000 for both; Euclidean
was unaffected, which is why every existing test passed.

Distance functions now return typed Distance or Similarity, and ordering goes
through a Closeness key that only they can build, so a raw similarity can no
longer reach a comparison. Removes the duplicate HeapOrder in the linear path
and the unused MaxHeapQueue. SIFT recall now runs on all three metrics.

* Format generated replication proto code in build.rs

Regeneration produced an unformatted diff against the committed files, so any
build dirtied the tree and the CI codegen check failed. Mirrors what
types/build.rs already does.

fix(replication): fsync raft log and vote writes before reporting success

RocksDB's default WriteOptions return once the record is in the OS page
cache. Openraft treats a successful storage call as proof the data is on
disk and advances commit on that basis, so the guarantee it relies on did
not hold for the log store.

Two failure modes on power loss or kernel panic (a clean shutdown is fine):

- A lost vote lets the node grant its vote twice in the same term, so two
  candidates can each collect a majority in that term.
- Lost entries drop data the leader already acknowledged to the client after
  a quorum, including this node, reported the append durable.

Every durable-state write in RocksLogStore now goes through sync_write_opts().
append_to_log_sync and the two delete loops also switch from per-key calls to
a single WriteBatch, so an append costs one fsync per batch instead of one per
entry. The deletes need durability too: if a crash loses a truncation the
conflicting tail reappears and get_log_state reports a last_log_id this node
never accepted from the current leader.
